NEW ORLEANS — New Orleans 1923. King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band —
Oliver and the young Louis Armstrong on cornets, Johnny Dodds's
clarinet, Honoré Dutrey's trombone — cutting "Dipper Mouth Blues"
in 1923: the collectively-improvising New Orleans front line, on
record, at full strength. THE SIDES WERE CUT IN RICHMOND, INDIANA
AND CHICAGO — the band had gone north with the Great Migration —
and the label says New Orleans anyway because the MUSIC is the
city's, the Kinshasa/Léopoldville rule applied in reverse: one
city per music, the recording trip in the comment. `jazz` (New
York 1945) and `swing` (Kansas City 1938) have both wanted "new
orleans jazz" since their lineages were written — bebop's whole
harmonic engine and the riff band's ensemble shout both walk out
of this polyphony — and both take it as a parent today.
THE AXES: CAST and DEVELOPMENT are one fact here — THREE lines at
once, each with its own job (lead states, clarinet weaves above,
trombone tailgates below), which is counterpoint reinvented by
ear in a dance hall. The word schedule below is those jobs.

the row's own cast: "THREE lines at once" — lead, clarinet, trombone

LINEAGE: `ragtime` (Sedalia 1899) is the repertory and the
syncopation the horns played off; `spirituals` (Nashville 1871)
is the church half of the city's ear. The brass band funerals
and the pre-electric blues are named below — the blues anchor
this table has is Chicago 1952, a CHILD of this music, and an
edge may not run backwards (the jumpblues/blues cycle rule).

THE MODE THIS RECORD CANNOT SOUND (2026-09-02, the catalogue round,
shift 2; test/precompose.test.js G14b).
King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, "Dipper Mouth Blues", cut 6 April 1923 —
this row's own record. Its roots are the blues I-IV-V (degrees 0, 3, 4) and
never degree 6, so mixolydian reached nothing; see the ruling written out in
full at `zydeco`. SCALES.blues on this same line is where the flat seventh
actually sounds, and it is untouched.

two-beat: the bass drum on 1 and 3, the snare's press on 2 and
4, the ride's woodblock chatter on the p lane.

CLOSEST, ANSWERED 2026-09-03 (the catalogue round, shift 3). The QA report's
`closest` column ranks each declared parent against every older row by a FEATURE
VECTOR — bpm, swing, major/minor, kit density, harmony kind, plan, nobass,
instrumental, family — and calls a parent sitting in the further half of that
ranking suspect. The vector has no term for the thing a child actually TAKES
from a parent, so an ancestor the record deliberately departs from ranks far by
construction, and the catalogue's trunk rows — funk, jazz, swing, ballad,
ambient, punk, drone, gregorian — rank far from nearly every leaf they grew.
THE PARENTS ON THIS ROW STAND. What the vector cannot see: `spirituals` is the VOICE and the collective heterophony that becomes the front
line's polyphony, and the vector reads an unaccompanied congregation against a
brass band. `musette` (1880) is offered as nearer on tempo and a wind-led band,
and Paris did not teach Storyville how to play.
label: New Orleans 1923
cannot: collective improvisation itself — three players making it up AT ONCE, listening to each other; the word schedule below fixes each voice's job per section, which is the texture with the conversation composed out (the fugue's own limit, a century over)
